## Chapter Roadmap {.compact}

:::: {.three-col}
::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">1 - Key Distributions</span>
Normal, Chi-square, Student's $t$, and $F$. Shape, parameters, and when each appears.
:::
::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">2 - Sampling Distributions</span>
Statistics have distributions too. The CLT explains why the sample mean is (approximately) normal for large $n$.
:::
::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">3 - Law of Large Numbers</span>
Sample averages converge to the true mean. The mathematical bridge from data to probability.
:::
::::

<br>

:::: {.three-col}
::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">Core skill</span>
Identify which distribution applies and read probability from it.
:::
::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">Core tool</span>
R functions `pnorm()`, `qnorm()`, `pchisq()`, `pt()`, `pf()`.
:::
::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">Core habit</span>
Check the degrees of freedom before looking up any critical value.
:::
::::

## What is Statistical Inference?

::: {.defbox .fragment}
**Statistical Inference**

The aim is to produce **estimators** of population parameters based on a smaller sample, and to quantify the accuracy of those estimators via a probability statement.

We collect data from a **sample** → compute **statistics** → make statements about the **population**.
:::

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.examplebox .fragment}
**Classic inferential question**

"How sure are we that the sample mean $\bar{x}$ is close to the true population mean $\mu$?"
:::
::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
**Why not measure everyone?**

Populations are usually infinite, very large, or expensive to enumerate. Sampling + inference is the practical solution.
:::
::::

---

## In-Class Example: Parameter, Statistic, and Sampling Variability {.scrollable}

:::: {.two-col-wide}
::: {.col}
::: {.taskbox}
<span class="label">In-Class Example</span>
Suppose the true average commute time for all UTM students is unknown.

A researcher takes **five different samples**, each with $n=25$ students, and computes a sample mean commute time for each sample.

**(a)** What is the population parameter?

**(b)** What statistic is computed from each sample?

**(c)** Why are the five sample means not exactly the same?

**(d)** What would happen to the sample means if each sample used $n=200$ students instead?
:::
:::

::: {.col}
```{r}
#| fig-width: 5.8
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-align: center
#| echo: false

set.seed(258)

sample_id <- rep(paste("Sample", 1:5), each = 25)
commute <- unlist(replicate(5, rgamma(25, shape = 5, scale = 8), simplify = FALSE))

df_commute <- data.frame(sample_id = sample_id, commute = commute)
means_commute <- aggregate(commute ~ sample_id, data = df_commute, FUN = mean)

ggplot(df_commute, aes(x = sample_id, y = commute)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.12, alpha = 0.55, colour = "#00695c", size = 1.8) +
  geom_point(data = means_commute,
             aes(x = sample_id, y = commute),
             colour = "#f9a825", size = 4) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Commute time (minutes)") +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```
:::
::::

## Sampling Variability - Check in R

```{webr}
#| autorun: false

set.seed(258)

sample_means <- replicate(5, {
  commute <- rgamma(25, shape = 5, scale = 8)
  mean(commute)
})

sample_means
mean(sample_means)
sd(sample_means)

# Try changing 25 to 200 and compare the spread of the sample means.
```

## 4.1 The Normal Distribution

:::: {.two-col-lean}
::: {.col}
::: {.defbox}
**Normal Distribution** — $X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)$

$$f(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} \cdot \exp\!\left(-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)$$

for $-\infty < x < \infty$.

Parameters: mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2 > 0$.
:::

::: {.examplebox .fragment}
Also called the **Gaussian distribution**, after Carl Friedrich Gauss (1809). It is symmetric and bell-shaped, completely characterized by $\mu$ and $\sigma$.
:::
:::

::: {.col}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5.5
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-align: center
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(data.frame(x = c(-6, 10)), aes(x)) +
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = -2, sd = 0.5),
                aes(colour = "N(-2, 0.5²)"), size = 1.3, geom = "area",
                fill = "#00BA38", alpha = 0.4, n = 500) +
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = 0, sd = 1),
                aes(colour = "N(0, 1²)"), size = 1.3, geom = "area",
                fill = "#F8766D", alpha = 0.4, n = 500) +
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = 3, sd = 1.5),
                aes(colour = "N(3, 1.5²)"), size = 1.3, geom = "area",
                fill = "#619CFF", alpha = 0.4, n = 500) +
  scale_colour_manual("", values = c("N(-2, 0.5²)" = "#00BA38",
                                     "N(0, 1²)"   = "#F8766D",
                                     "N(3, 1.5²)" = "#619CFF")) +
  labs(x = "x", y = "Density") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(), legend.position = "top",
        legend.text = element_text(size = 9))
```
:::
::::

---

## 4.1.1 The Standard Normal Distribution

::: {.defbox .fragment}
**Standard Normal** — $Z \sim N(0, 1)$

$$f(z) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \cdot e^{-z^2/2}$$

A special case with $\mu = 0$ and $\sigma^2 = 1$. Denoted $Z$.
:::

::: {.examplebox .fragment}
**Standardising.** Any $X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)$ can be converted:

$$Z = \frac{X - \mu}{\sigma} \sim N(0,1)$$

This lets us use a single table (or `pnorm()`) for any normal distribution.
:::

## Empirical Rule — Interactive Explorer

<div id="emp-rule-box" style="border:1px solid #d8dee2; border-radius:10px; padding:12px 16px; background:white; font-size:0.72em;">

<div style="display:grid; grid-template-columns:1fr 1fr; gap:18px; margin-bottom:10px;">

<div>
<label style="font-weight:800; color:#004d40; font-size:1.05em;">
Mean (μ): <span id="emp-mu-label">0</span>
</label>
<input
  id="emp-mu-slider"
  type="range"
  min="-5"
  max="5"
  step="0.5"
  value="0"
  oninput="empRuleUpdate()"
  style="width:100%; accent-color:#00695c; margin-top:8px;"
>
</div>

<div>
<label style="font-weight:800; color:#004d40; font-size:1.05em;">
Standard deviation (σ): <span id="emp-sd-label">1</span>
</label>
<input
  id="emp-sd-slider"
  type="range"
  min="0.5"
  max="3"
  step="0.25"
  value="1"
  oninput="empRuleUpdate()"
  style="width:100%; accent-color:#00695c; margin-top:8px;"
>
</div>

</div>

<canvas id="emp-rule-canvas" width="1100" height="310" style="width:100%; height:260px; display:block;"></canvas>

<div style="display:grid; grid-template-columns:repeat(3,1fr); gap:8px; margin-top:10px; text-align:center;">

<div style="background:rgba(0,105,92,0.13); border-radius:7px; padding:8px 0; font-weight:800; font-size:1.25em;">
μ ± 1σ<br>68.27%
</div>

<div style="background:rgba(0,176,246,0.15); border-radius:7px; padding:8px 0; font-weight:800; font-size:1.25em;">
μ ± 2σ<br>95.45%
</div>

<div style="background:rgba(121,151,255,0.17); border-radius:7px; padding:8px 0; font-weight:800; font-size:1.25em;">
μ ± 3σ<br>99.73%
</div>

</div>

</div>

<script>
window.empRuleUpdate = function () {
  var canvas = document.getElementById("emp-rule-canvas");
  var muSlider = document.getElementById("emp-mu-slider");
  var sdSlider = document.getElementById("emp-sd-slider");
  var muLabel = document.getElementById("emp-mu-label");
  var sdLabel = document.getElementById("emp-sd-label");

  if (!canvas || !muSlider || !sdSlider || !muLabel || !sdLabel) {
    return;
  }

  var mu = Number(muSlider.value);
  var sd = Number(sdSlider.value);

  muLabel.innerHTML = mu;
  sdLabel.innerHTML = sd;

  var ctx = canvas.getContext("2d");
  var width = canvas.width;
  var height = canvas.height;

  ctx.clearRect(0, 0, width, height);

  function dnorm(x, mean, sigma) {
    return Math.exp(-0.5 * Math.pow((x - mean) / sigma, 2)) / (sigma * Math.sqrt(2 * Math.PI));
  }

  var marginLeft = 65;
  var marginRight = 30;
  var marginTop = 20;
  var marginBottom = 55;

  var plotWidth = width - marginLeft - marginRight;
  var plotHeight = height - marginTop - marginBottom;

  /* FIXED AXIS: this is the important change */
  var xmin = -15;
  var xmax = 15;
  var ymax = 0.85;

  function xScale(x) {
    return marginLeft + ((x - xmin) / (xmax - xmin)) * plotWidth;
  }

  function yScale(y) {
    return marginTop + (1 - y / ymax) * plotHeight;
  }

  function shade(a, b, color) {
    var start = Math.max(a, xmin);
    var end = Math.min(b, xmax);

    if (end <= xmin || start >= xmax) {
      return;
    }

    ctx.beginPath();
    ctx.moveTo(xScale(start), yScale(0));

    for (var i = 0; i <= 300; i++) {
      var x = start + (end - start) * i / 300;
      var y = dnorm(x, mu, sd);
      ctx.lineTo(xScale(x), yScale(y));
    }

    ctx.lineTo(xScale(end), yScale(0));
    ctx.closePath();
    ctx.fillStyle = color;
    ctx.fill();
  }

  /* grid lines */
  ctx.strokeStyle = "#e5e7eb";
  ctx.lineWidth = 1;

  for (var g = 0; g <= 4; g++) {
    var gy = marginTop + (plotHeight * g) / 4;
    ctx.beginPath();
    ctx.moveTo(marginLeft, gy);
    ctx.lineTo(width - marginRight, gy);
    ctx.stroke();
  }

  /* shade empirical regions */
  shade(mu - 3 * sd, mu + 3 * sd, "rgba(121,151,255,0.22)");
  shade(mu - 2 * sd, mu + 2 * sd, "rgba(0,176,246,0.28)");
  shade(mu - 1 * sd, mu + 1 * sd, "rgba(0,105,92,0.35)");

  /* curve */
  ctx.beginPath();
  ctx.strokeStyle = "#004d40";
  ctx.lineWidth = 3;

  for (var j = 0; j <= 900; j++) {
    var xVal = xmin + (xmax - xmin) * j / 900;
    var yVal = dnorm(xVal, mu, sd);

    if (j === 0) {
      ctx.moveTo(xScale(xVal), yScale(yVal));
    } else {
      ctx.lineTo(xScale(xVal), yScale(yVal));
    }
  }

  ctx.stroke();

  /* x-axis */
  ctx.beginPath();
  ctx.strokeStyle = "#555";
  ctx.lineWidth = 1.5;
  ctx.moveTo(marginLeft, yScale(0));
  ctx.lineTo(width - marginRight, yScale(0));
  ctx.stroke();

  /* mean line */
  ctx.beginPath();
  ctx.strokeStyle = "#f9a825";
  ctx.lineWidth = 1.5;
  ctx.setLineDash([6, 6]);
  ctx.moveTo(xScale(mu), marginTop);
  ctx.lineTo(xScale(mu), yScale(0));
  ctx.stroke();
  ctx.setLineDash([]);

  /* fixed number axis labels */
  ctx.fillStyle = "#2f3437";
  ctx.font = "14px Arial";
  ctx.textAlign = "center";

  for (var tick = -10; tick <= 10; tick += 2) {
    ctx.fillText(tick, xScale(tick), height - 18);
  }

  /* sigma labels above axis */
  var labels = [
    { x: mu - 3 * sd, text: "μ - 3σ" },
    { x: mu - 2 * sd, text: "μ - 2σ" },
    { x: mu - 1 * sd, text: "μ - σ" },
    { x: mu,          text: "μ" },
    { x: mu + 1 * sd, text: "μ + σ" },
    { x: mu + 2 * sd, text: "μ + 2σ" },
    { x: mu + 3 * sd, text: "μ + 3σ" }
  ];

  ctx.font = "12px Arial";

  for (var k = 0; k < labels.length; k++) {
    if (labels[k].x >= xmin && labels[k].x <= xmax) {
      ctx.fillText(labels[k].text, xScale(labels[k].x), height - 35);
    }
  }
};

setTimeout(window.empRuleUpdate, 200);
setTimeout(window.empRuleUpdate, 700);

if (window.Reveal) {
  Reveal.on("slidechanged", function () {
    setTimeout(window.empRuleUpdate, 150);
  });
}
</script>

## Normal Probabilities in R

:::: {.two-col-lean}
::: {.col}
```{webr}
#| autorun: false

# P(Z <= 1.96)
pnorm(1.96)

# P(Z > 1.96)   (right tail)
pnorm(1.96, lower.tail = FALSE)

# P(-1.96 < Z < 1.96)
pnorm(1.96) - pnorm(-1.96)

# Critical value: find z such that P(Z <= z) = 0.975
qnorm(0.975)
```
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.examplebox}
**`pnorm(q, mean, sd)`** gives $P(X \le q)$.

**`qnorm(p, mean, sd)`** inverts: gives $q$ such that $P(X \le q) = p$.

Default: `mean = 0`, `sd = 1` (standard normal).
:::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
**Try it.** What is $P(X < 130)$ when $X \sim N(100, 15^2)$? Use `pnorm(130, mean = 100, sd = 15)`.
:::
:::
::::

## In-Class Example: Normal Probability with a Plot {.scrollable}

:::: {.two-col-wide}
::: {.col}
::: {.taskbox}
<span class="label">In-Class Example</span>
Suppose final exam scores are approximately normal with mean $\mu=72$ and standard deviation $\sigma=8$.

**(a)** Find the $z$-score for a score of $84$.

**(b)** Find $P(X \le 84)$.

**(c)** Find $P(X > 84)$.

**(d)** On the plot, identify the shaded right-tail region and explain why it represents $P(X > 84)$.
:::
:::

::: {.col}
```{r}
#| fig-width: 5.8
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-align: center
#| echo: false

mu <- 72
sigma <- 8
cutoff <- 84

x <- seq(mu - 4*sigma, mu + 4*sigma, length.out = 1000)
df_norm <- data.frame(x = x, density = dnorm(x, mean = mu, sd = sigma))

ggplot(df_norm, aes(x, density)) +
  geom_area(data = subset(df_norm, x >= cutoff),
            fill = "#fff8e1", alpha = 0.9) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1, colour = "#00695c") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mu, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#004d40", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = cutoff, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#f9a825", linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("text", x = mu, y = 0.048, label = "Mean = 72", colour = "#004d40", fontface = "bold") +
  annotate("text", x = cutoff + 4, y = 0.025, label = "P(X > 84)", colour = "#f9a825", fontface = "bold") +
  labs(x = "Exam score", y = "Density") +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```
:::

```{webr}
x <- 84

z

pnorm(x, mean = mu, sd = sigma)       # P(X <= 84)
1 - pnorm(x, mean = mu, sd = sigma)   # P(X > 84)
```

## Heights — Check in R with Plot

```{webr}
#| autorun: false

mu <- 170
sigma <- 8

# (a) P(X < 180)
pnorm(180, mean = mu, sd = sigma)

# (b) P(X > 160)
pnorm(160, mean = mu, sd = sigma, lower.tail = FALSE)

# (c) P(162 < X < 178)
pnorm(178, mean = mu, sd = sigma) - pnorm(162, mean = mu, sd = sigma)

# (d) 95th percentile because only 5% are above
qnorm(0.95, mean = mu, sd = sigma)

# Plot the normal distribution and shade part (c)
x <- seq(mu - 4*sigma, mu + 4*sigma, length.out = 1000)
y <- dnorm(x, mean = mu, sd = sigma)

plot(x, y,
     type = "l",
     lwd = 2,
     col = "#00695c",
     xlab = "Height in cm",
     ylab = "Density",
     main = "Normal model for adult heights")

shade_x <- x[x >= 162 & x <= 178]
shade_y <- dnorm(shade_x, mean = mu, sd = sigma)

polygon(c(162, shade_x, 178),
        c(0, shade_y, 0),
        col = "#c8e6f3",
        border = NA)

lines(x, y, lwd = 2, col = "#00695c")
abline(v = mu, lty = 2, col = "#004d40", lwd = 2)
abline(v = c(160, 162, 178, 180), lty = 2, col = "#f9a825")
```

:::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## Visual Question

The Empirical Rule says the middle region from $-2$ to $2$ contains about 95.45% of the standard normal curve. Using symmetry, what is $P(Z > 2)$?
::::

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8.6
#| fig-height: 2.05
#| fig-align: center
#| echo: false

z <- seq(-4, 4, length.out = 1000)
df_emp_q <- data.frame(z = z, density = dnorm(z))

ggplot(df_emp_q, aes(z, density)) +
  geom_area(data = subset(df_emp_q, z >= -2 & z <= 2),
            fill = "#c8e6f3", alpha = 0.9) +
  geom_area(data = subset(df_emp_q, z > 2),
            fill = "#f9a825", alpha = 0.9) +
  geom_area(data = subset(df_emp_q, z < -2),
            fill = "#fff8e1", alpha = 0.9) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1, colour = "#00695c") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-2, 2), linetype = "dashed",
             colour = "#004d40", linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("text", x = 0, y = 0.22, label = "Middle area ≈ 0.9545",
           colour = "#004d40", fontface = "bold", size = 3.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 2.7, y = 0.06, label = "Right tail?",
           colour = "#f9a825", fontface = "bold", size = 3.5) +
  labs(title = "Standard normal symmetry",
       x = "z", y = "Density") +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))
```

- 0.9545
- 0.0455
- [0.02275]{.correct data-explanation="The total area outside -2 to 2 is 1 - 0.9545 = 0.0455. By symmetry, each tail has area 0.0455 divided by 2, which is 0.02275."}
- 0.0500

## 4.1.2 The Chi-Square Distribution

::: {.defbox}
**Chi-Square Random Variable** — $X \sim \chi^2_k$

If $Z_1, Z_2, \ldots, Z_k \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} N(0,1)$, then

$$X = \sum_{i=1}^{k} Z_i^2 \sim \chi^2_k$$

The pdf for $x > 0$ is:

$$f(x; k) = \frac{1}{2^{k/2}\,\Gamma(k/2)}\, x^{k/2 - 1}\, e^{-x/2}$$
:::

::: {.examplebox .fragment}
The distribution is **right-skewed** and supported on $(0, \infty)$. As $k$ increases, it becomes more symmetric.  $E[X] = k$, $\text{Var}(X) = 2k$.
:::

---

## Chi-Square: Shape by Degrees of Freedom

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-align: center
library(ggplot2)
x_vals <- seq(0.01, 25, length.out = 600)
df_plot <- rbind(
  data.frame(x = x_vals, y = dchisq(x_vals, df=2),  dist = "χ²(2)"),
  data.frame(x = x_vals, y = dchisq(x_vals, df=5),  dist = "χ²(5)"),
  data.frame(x = x_vals, y = dchisq(x_vals, df=10), dist = "χ²(10)")
)
ggplot(df_plot, aes(x, y, colour=dist, fill=dist)) +
  geom_area(alpha=0.4, position="identity") +
  geom_line(size=1.2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values=c("#00BA38","#F8766D","#619CFF")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values=c("#00BA38","#F8766D","#619CFF")) +
  labs(x="x", y="Density", colour=NULL, fill=NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size=12) +
  theme(panel.grid=element_blank(), legend.position="top")
```

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
**Key fact.** The chi-square distribution is always positive and right-skewed. It plays a central role in tests for variance and for categorical data (Chapter 7+).
:::

---

## Chi-Square in R

:::: {.two-col-lean}
::: {.col}
```{webr}
#| autorun: false

# P(X <= 10) where X ~ chi-sq(5)
pchisq(10, df = 5)

# Upper tail: P(X > 10)
pchisq(10, df = 5, lower.tail = FALSE)

# Critical value: 95th percentile with df=10
qchisq(0.95, df = 10)

# Plot the distribution
curve(dchisq(x, df = 5), from = 0, to = 20,
      col = "#F8766D", lwd = 2,
      main = "Chi-Square(5)", ylab = "Density")
```
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.defbox}
**Mean & Variance**

For $X \sim \chi^2_k$:

$$E[X] = k, \qquad \text{Var}(X) = 2k$$

As $k \to \infty$, the chi-square distribution approaches a normal distribution (by the CLT).
:::
:::
::::

**(a)** Find $P(X \leq 15.507)$.

**(b)** Find the 95th percentile of $X$.

**(c)** If $Z_1, Z_2, Z_3 \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} N(0,1)$, what is the distribution of $Z_1^2 + Z_2^2 + Z_3^2$?

## Chi-Square Example — Check in R with Plot

```{webr}
#| autorun: false

# Let X ~ chi-square with df = 8
df_value <- 8
cutoff <- 15.507

# (a) P(X <= 15.507)
pchisq(cutoff, df = df_value)

# (b) 95th percentile
qchisq(0.95, df = df_value)

# (c) sum of 3 squared standard normals is chi-square with 3 df

# (d) mean = k, variance = 2k
cat("Mean:", df_value, "  Variance:", 2 * df_value, "\n")

# Plot and shade P(X <= 15.507)
x <- seq(0, 30, length.out = 1000)
y <- dchisq(x, df = df_value)

plot(x, y,
     type = "l",
     lwd = 2,
     col = "#00695c",
     xlab = "x",
     ylab = "Density",
     main = "Chi-square distribution with 8 df")

shade_x <- x[x <= cutoff]
shade_y <- dchisq(shade_x, df = df_value)

polygon(c(0, shade_x, cutoff),
        c(0, shade_y, 0),
        col = "#c8e6f3",
        border = NA)

lines(x, y, lwd = 2, col = "#00695c")
abline(v = cutoff, lty = 2, col = "#f9a825", lwd = 2)
```

## Example

$Z_1, Z_2, Z_3, Z_4 \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} N(0,1)$. What is the distribution of

$$W = Z_1^2 + Z_2^2 + Z_3^2 + Z_4^2 \; ?$$
::::

- $W \sim N(0,4)$
- $W \sim \chi^2_2$
- [$W \sim \chi^2_4$]{.correct data-explanation="The sum of squares of k independent standard normal variables has a chi-square distribution with k degrees of freedom. Here k = 4."}
- $W \sim t_4$

## 4.1.3 The Student's $t$-Distribution

::: {.defbox}
**Student's $t$ Distribution** — $T \sim t_\nu$

If $Z \sim N(0,1)$ and $U \sim \chi^2_\nu$ are **independent**, then

$$T = \frac{Z}{\sqrt{U/\nu}} \sim t_\nu$$

The pdf is:

$$f_T(t;\nu) = \frac{\Gamma\!\left(\frac{\nu+1}{2}\right)}{\sqrt{\pi\nu}\,\Gamma\!\left(\frac{\nu}{2}\right)} \left(1 + \frac{t^2}{\nu}\right)^{-\frac{\nu+1}{2}}, \quad -\infty < t < \infty$$
:::

::: {.warnbox .fragment}
The $t$-distribution has **heavier tails** than the normal. As $\nu \to \infty$, $t_\nu \to N(0,1)$.
:::

---

## $t$ vs Normal: Heavier Tails

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-align: center
x_vals <- seq(-4, 4, length.out = 400)
df_t <- rbind(
  data.frame(x=x_vals, y=dnorm(x_vals),       dist="Standard Normal"),
  data.frame(x=x_vals, y=dt(x_vals, df=2),    dist="t(2)"),
  data.frame(x=x_vals, y=dt(x_vals, df=9),    dist="t(9)")
)
ggplot(df_t, aes(x, y, colour=dist, linetype=dist)) +
  geom_line(size=1.3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values=c("#F8766D","#00BA38","#619CFF")) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values=c("solid","dashed","dashed")) +
  labs(x="t", y="Density", colour=NULL, linetype=NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size=12) +
  theme(panel.grid=element_blank(), legend.position="top")
```

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
**Why does this matter?** When estimating a mean from a small sample with unknown $\sigma$, we use $t$ critical values — they are larger than $z$ values, reflecting extra uncertainty.
:::

## $t$-Distribution: Interactive Tail Comparison

<div id="t-tail-box" style="border:1px solid #d8dee2; border-radius:10px; padding:12px 16px; background:white; font-size:0.72em;">

<div style="display:grid; grid-template-columns:1fr 1fr; gap:18px; margin-bottom:10px;">

<div>
<label style="font-weight:800; color:#004d40; font-size:1.05em;">
Degrees of Freedom (ν): <span id="t-df-label">5</span>
</label>
<input
  id="t-df-slider"
  type="range"
  min="2"
  max="50"
  step="1"
  value="5"
  oninput="tTailUpdate()"
  style="width:100%; accent-color:#00695c; margin-top:8px;"
>
</div>

<div>
<label style="font-weight:800; color:#004d40; font-size:1.05em;">
Tail cutoff (c): <span id="t-cutoff-label">2</span>
</label>
<input
  id="t-cutoff-slider"
  type="range"
  min="0.5"
  max="4"
  step="0.1"
  value="2"
  oninput="tTailUpdate()"
  style="width:100%; accent-color:#00695c; margin-top:8px;"
>
</div>

</div>

<canvas id="t-tail-canvas" width="1100" height="310" style="width:100%; height:260px; display:block;"></canvas>

<div style="display:grid; grid-template-columns:1fr 1fr; gap:10px; margin-top:10px; text-align:center;">

<div id="t-tail-readout" style="background:rgba(97,156,255,0.13); border-radius:7px; padding:8px 0; font-weight:800; font-size:1.25em;">
P(|T| &gt; 2) = —
</div>

<div id="z-tail-readout" style="background:rgba(248,118,109,0.13); border-radius:7px; padding:8px 0; font-weight:800; font-size:1.25em;">
P(|Z| &gt; 2) = —
</div>

</div>

</div>

<script>
window.tTailUpdate = function () {
  var canvas = document.getElementById("t-tail-canvas");
  var dfSlider = document.getElementById("t-df-slider");
  var cutoffSlider = document.getElementById("t-cutoff-slider");
  var dfLabel = document.getElementById("t-df-label");
  var cutoffLabel = document.getElementById("t-cutoff-label");
  var tReadout = document.getElementById("t-tail-readout");
  var zReadout = document.getElementById("z-tail-readout");

  if (!canvas || !dfSlider || !cutoffSlider || !dfLabel || !cutoffLabel || !tReadout || !zReadout) {
    return;
  }

  var nu = Number(dfSlider.value);
  var cutoff = Number(cutoffSlider.value);

  dfLabel.innerHTML = nu;
  cutoffLabel.innerHTML = cutoff.toFixed(1);

  var ctx = canvas.getContext("2d");
  var width = canvas.width;
  var height = canvas.height;

  ctx.clearRect(0, 0, width, height);

  function logGamma(z) {
    var x = [
      57.1562356658629235,
      -59.5979603554754912,
      14.1360979747417471,
      -0.491913816097620199,
      0.339946499848118887e-4,
      0.465236289270485756e-4,
      -0.983744753048795646e-4,
      0.158088703224912494e-3,
      -0.210264441724104883e-3,
      0.217439618115212643e-3,
      -0.164318106536763890e-3,
      0.844182239838527433e-4,
      -0.261908384015814087e-4,
      0.368991826595316234e-5
    ];

    var y = z;
    var tmp = z + 5.2421875;
    tmp = (z + 0.5) * Math.log(tmp) - tmp;

    var ser = 0.999999999999997092;

    for (var j = 0; j < x.length; j++) {
      ser += x[j] / ++y;
    }

    return tmp + Math.log(2.5066282746310005 * ser / z);
  }

  function tDensity(x, df) {
    var a = logGamma((df + 1) / 2);
    var b = logGamma(df / 2);
    var c = Math.sqrt(df * Math.PI);
    var d = Math.pow(1 + (x * x) / df, -(df + 1) / 2);

    return Math.exp(a - b) * d / c;
  }

  function normalDensity(x) {
    return Math.exp(-0.5 * x * x) / Math.sqrt(2 * Math.PI);
  }

  function approxTwoTailT(df, c) {
    var step = 0.002;
    var area = 0;

    for (var x = c; x <= 20; x += step) {
      area += tDensity(x, df) * step;
    }

    return 2 * area;
  }

  function erf(x) {
    var sign = x >= 0 ? 1 : -1;
    x = Math.abs(x);

    var a1 = 0.254829592;
    var a2 = -0.284496736;
    var a3 = 1.421413741;
    var a4 = -1.453152027;
    var a5 = 1.061405429;
    var p = 0.3275911;

    var t = 1 / (1 + p * x);
    var y = 1 - (((((a5 * t + a4) * t) + a3) * t + a2) * t + a1) * t * Math.exp(-x * x);

    return sign * y;
  }

  function normalCdf(x) {
    return 0.5 * (1 + erf(x / Math.sqrt(2)));
  }

  function approxTwoTailZ(c) {
    return 2 * (1 - normalCdf(c));
  }

  var marginLeft = 65;
  var marginRight = 30;
  var marginTop = 20;
  var marginBottom = 55;

  var plotWidth = width - marginLeft - marginRight;
  var plotHeight = height - marginTop - marginBottom;

  /* Fixed axis so the curve visibly changes */
  var xmin = -6;
  var xmax = 6;
  var ymax = 0.45;

  function xScale(x) {
    return marginLeft + ((x - xmin) / (xmax - xmin)) * plotWidth;
  }

  function yScale(y) {
    return marginTop + (1 - y / ymax) * plotHeight;
  }

  function shadeTail(left, right, densityFun, color) {
    ctx.beginPath();
    ctx.moveTo(xScale(left), yScale(0));

    for (var i = 0; i <= 300; i++) {
      var x = left + (right - left) * i / 300;
      var y = densityFun(x);
      ctx.lineTo(xScale(x), yScale(y));
    }

    ctx.lineTo(xScale(right), yScale(0));
    ctx.closePath();
    ctx.fillStyle = color;
    ctx.fill();
  }

  /* Grid */
  ctx.strokeStyle = "#e5e7eb";
  ctx.lineWidth = 1;

  for (var grid = 0; grid <= 4; grid++) {
    var yGrid = marginTop + (plotHeight * grid) / 4;
    ctx.beginPath();
    ctx.moveTo(marginLeft, yGrid);
    ctx.lineTo(width - marginRight, yGrid);
    ctx.stroke();
  }

  /* Shade t tails */
  shadeTail(xmin, -cutoff, function (x) { return tDensity(x, nu); }, "rgba(97,156,255,0.22)");
  shadeTail(cutoff, xmax, function (x) { return tDensity(x, nu); }, "rgba(97,156,255,0.22)");

  /* Normal curve */
  ctx.beginPath();
  ctx.strokeStyle = "#f8766d";
  ctx.lineWidth = 2.4;

  for (var i = 0; i <= 900; i++) {
    var xNorm = xmin + (xmax - xmin) * i / 900;
    var yNorm = normalDensity(xNorm);

    if (i === 0) {
      ctx.moveTo(xScale(xNorm), yScale(yNorm));
    } else {
      ctx.lineTo(xScale(xNorm), yScale(yNorm));
    }
  }

  ctx.stroke();

  /* t curve */
  ctx.beginPath();
  ctx.strokeStyle = "#619cff";
  ctx.lineWidth = 2.8;

  for (var j = 0; j <= 900; j++) {
    var xT = xmin + (xmax - xmin) * j / 900;
    var yT = tDensity(xT, nu);

    if (j === 0) {
      ctx.moveTo(xScale(xT), yScale(yT));
    } else {
      ctx.lineTo(xScale(xT), yScale(yT));
    }
  }

  ctx.stroke();

  /* X-axis */
  ctx.beginPath();
  ctx.strokeStyle = "#555";
  ctx.lineWidth = 1.5;
  ctx.moveTo(marginLeft, yScale(0));
  ctx.lineTo(width - marginRight, yScale(0));
  ctx.stroke();

  /* Cutoff lines */
  ctx.beginPath();
  ctx.strokeStyle = "#f9a825";
  ctx.lineWidth = 1.5;
  ctx.setLineDash([6, 6]);
  ctx.moveTo(xScale(-cutoff), marginTop);
  ctx.lineTo(xScale(-cutoff), yScale(0));
  ctx.moveTo(xScale(cutoff), marginTop);
  ctx.lineTo(xScale(cutoff), yScale(0));
  ctx.stroke();
  ctx.setLineDash([]);

  /* Axis labels */
  ctx.fillStyle = "#2f3437";
  ctx.font = "14px Arial";
  ctx.textAlign = "center";

  for (var tick = -6; tick <= 6; tick += 1) {
    ctx.fillText(tick, xScale(tick), height - 18);
  }

  /* Legend */
  ctx.textAlign = "left";
  ctx.font = "16px Arial";

  ctx.strokeStyle = "#f8766d";
  ctx.lineWidth = 4;
  ctx.beginPath();
  ctx.moveTo(marginLeft + 10, marginTop + 18);
  ctx.lineTo(marginLeft + 45, marginTop + 18);
  ctx.stroke();

  ctx.fillStyle = "#2f3437";
  ctx.fillText("N(0,1)", marginLeft + 52, marginTop + 23);

  ctx.strokeStyle = "#619cff";
  ctx.lineWidth = 4;
  ctx.beginPath();
  ctx.moveTo(marginLeft + 10, marginTop + 42);
  ctx.lineTo(marginLeft + 45, marginTop + 42);
  ctx.stroke();

  ctx.fillStyle = "#2f3437";
  ctx.fillText("t(" + nu + ")", marginLeft + 52, marginTop + 47);

  var tTail = approxTwoTailT(nu, cutoff);
  var zTail = approxTwoTailZ(cutoff);

  tReadout.innerHTML = "P(|T| &gt; " + cutoff.toFixed(1) + ") = " + tTail.toFixed(4);
  zReadout.innerHTML = "P(|Z| &gt; " + cutoff.toFixed(1) + ") = " + zTail.toFixed(4);
};

setTimeout(window.tTailUpdate, 200);
setTimeout(window.tTailUpdate, 700);

if (window.Reveal) {
  Reveal.on("slidechanged", function () {
    setTimeout(window.tTailUpdate, 150);
  });
}
</script>

## $t$-Distribution in R

:::: {.two-col-lean}
::: {.col}
```{webr}
#| autorun: false

# P(T <= 2.0) with df = 10
pt(2.0, df = 10)

# Critical value: t such that P(T <= t) = 0.975, df=10
qt(0.975, df = 10)

# Compare to z critical value
qnorm(0.975)

# How many df until t ≈ z?
qt(0.975, df = c(5, 10, 30, 100, 1000))
```
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.examplebox}
**`pt(q, df)`** → $P(T \le q)$

**`qt(p, df)`** → inverse CDF

Notice `qt(0.975, df=10) = 2.228` vs `qnorm(0.975) = 1.960`. The $t$ critical value is larger — reflecting extra uncertainty in small samples.
:::
:::
::::

## $t$ Example — Check in R with Plot

```{webr}
#| autorun: false

# (a) P(T <= 2.131), df=15
pt(2.131, df = 15)

# (b) c such that P(-c <= T <= c) = 0.95, df=20
qt(0.975, df = 20)

# (c) P(|T| > 2.571), df=5
2 * pt(2.571, df = 5, lower.tail = FALSE)

# (d) 97.5th percentile comparison
qt(0.975, df = c(5, 30))
qnorm(0.975)

# Plot part (c): two tails for t with df = 5
df_value <- 5
cutoff <- 2.571

x <- seq(-5, 5, length.out = 1000)
y <- dt(x, df = df_value)

plot(x, y,
     type = "l",
     lwd = 2,
     col = "#00695c",
     xlab = "t",
     ylab = "Density",
     main = "Two-tail probability for t distribution")

left_x <- x[x <= -cutoff]
left_y <- dt(left_x, df = df_value)

right_x <- x[x >= cutoff]
right_y <- dt(right_x, df = df_value)

polygon(c(min(left_x), left_x, -cutoff),
        c(0, left_y, 0),
        col = "#c8e6f3",
        border = NA)

polygon(c(cutoff, right_x, max(right_x)),
        c(0, right_y, 0),
        col = "#c8e6f3",
        border = NA)

lines(x, y, lwd = 2, col = "#00695c")
abline(v = c(-cutoff, cutoff), lty = 2, col = "#f9a825", lwd = 2)
```

## Visual Question

The blue curve has heavier tails than the red normal curve. Why do we use the $t$-distribution instead of the normal for small-sample inference about a mean?
::::

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8.6
#| fig-height: 2.1
#| fig-align: center
#| echo: false

x_tq <- seq(-4, 4, length.out = 1000)
df_tq <- rbind(
  data.frame(x = x_tq, density = dnorm(x_tq), dist = "Normal"),
  data.frame(x = x_tq, density = dt(x_tq, df = 5), dist = "t with df = 5")
)

ggplot(df_tq, aes(x, density, colour = dist)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.25) +
  geom_area(data = subset(df_tq, dist == "t with df = 5" & abs(x) > 2),
            aes(x = x, y = density), inherit.aes = FALSE,
            fill = "#c8e6f3", alpha = 0.55) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Normal" = "#f8766d",
                                 "t with df = 5" = "#00695c"),
                      guide = "none") +
  annotate("text", x = -2.7, y = 0.045, label = "heavier tails",
           colour = "#00695c", fontface = "bold", size = 3.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 2.7, y = 0.045, label = "heavier tails",
           colour = "#00695c", fontface = "bold", size = 3.5) +
  labs(title = "Normal vs t distribution",
       subtitle = "Heavier tails account for extra uncertainty",
       x = "Value", y = "Density") +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))
```

- The $t$ is easier to compute
- [We must estimate $\sigma$ from the data, adding uncertainty — $t$ has heavier tails to account for this]{.correct data-explanation="Replacing unknown sigma with the sample standard deviation adds extra uncertainty. The t distribution has heavier tails than the normal, producing wider and more honest confidence intervals."}
- The normal distribution is only valid for large populations
- Small samples always have skewed data

## 4.1.4 The $F$-Distribution

::: {.defbox}
**$F$ Random Variable** — $F \sim F_{\nu_1, \nu_2}$

If $U \sim \chi^2_{\nu_1}$ and $V \sim \chi^2_{\nu_2}$ are **independent**, then

$$F = \frac{U/\nu_1}{V/\nu_2} \sim F_{\nu_1, \nu_2}$$

The $F$ distribution is supported on $(0, \infty)$ and characterised by two degrees of freedom: **numerator** $\nu_1$ and **denominator** $\nu_2$.
:::

::: {.examplebox .fragment}
The $F$ distribution is used to **compare two variances** and is the backbone of **ANOVA** (Analysis of Variance). You will see it a lot in later chapters.
:::

---

## Distribution Summary Table

| Distribution | Parameters | Support | $E[X]$ | Key use |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ | $\mu, \sigma^2$ | $\mathbb{R}$ | $\mu$ | General continuous |
| $\chi^2_k$ | $k$ (df) | $(0,\infty)$ | $k$ | Variance tests |
| $t_\nu$ | $\nu$ (df) | $\mathbb{R}$ | $0$ | Small-sample mean |
| $F_{\nu_1,\nu_2}$ | $\nu_1, \nu_2$ | $(0,\infty)$ | $\dfrac{\nu_2}{\nu_2-2}$ | Variance ratios |

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
**Connections.** $Z^2 \sim \chi^2_1$; $\;$ $t_\nu^2 \sim F_{1,\nu}$; $\;$ $t_\nu \to N(0,1)$ and $\chi^2_k/k \to 1$ as degrees of freedom grow.
:::

## 4.2 Sampling Distributions

::: {.defbox .fragment}
**Sampling Distribution**

The **probability distribution** of a statistic (such as $\bar{X}$) computed from all possible random samples of a given size $n$ drawn from the same population.
:::

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.examplebox .fragment}
**Key idea.** $\bar{X}$ is not a fixed number — it is a **random variable**. Each new sample of size $n$ gives a different value of $\bar{X}$. The sampling distribution describes how those values vary.
:::
::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
**Why it matters.** Understanding the variability of $\bar{X}$ from sample to sample is the foundation for confidence intervals and hypothesis tests.
:::
::::

---

## Sampling Distribution of $\bar{X}$

::: {.defbox}
**Distribution of the sample mean**

If $X_1, \ldots, X_n \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}$ population with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$, then:

$$E[\bar{X}] = \mu \qquad \text{Var}(\bar{X}) = \frac{\sigma^2}{n}$$

The **standard error** of $\bar{X}$ is $\text{SE}(\bar{X}) = \dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$.
:::

::: {.warnbox .fragment}
**Larger $n$ → smaller SE.** Collecting more data shrinks the variability of the sample mean. This is why bigger samples give more precise estimates.
:::

---

## Sampling Distribution — Simulation

```{webr}
#| autorun: false

# Simulate sampling distribution of X-bar
# Population: Exponential(rate=1), mu=1, sigma^2=1

n     <- 30      # sample size
reps  <- 5000    # number of samples

xbar_vals <- replicate(reps, mean(rexp(n, rate = 1)))

hist(xbar_vals, breaks = 50,
     col = "#00695c", border = "white",
     main = paste("Sampling distribution: n =", n),
     xlab = "Sample mean", freq = FALSE)

# Overlay theoretical normal
curve(dnorm(x, mean = 1, sd = 1/sqrt(n)),
      add = TRUE, col = "#F8766D", lwd = 2)
```

::: {.small-text}
Change `n` to 5 or 2 and re-run. Watch the distribution become less normal.
:::

## 4.3 The Central Limit Theorem

::: {.defbox}
**Central Limit Theorem (CLT)**

Let $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$ be i.i.d. with $E[X_i] = \mu$ and $\text{Var}(X_i) = \sigma^2 < \infty$. Then as $n \to \infty$:

$$\frac{\sqrt{n}(\bar{X}_n - \mu)}{\sigma} \;\overset{d}{\longrightarrow}\; N(0,1)$$

Equivalently, for large $n$: $\quad \bar{X}_n \;\dot{\sim}\; N\!\left(\mu,\, \frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right)$
:::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
**Remarkable.** The CLT holds for **any** parent distribution with finite variance — uniform, exponential, Poisson, or anything else. The shape of $\bar{X}$ approaches normal as $n$ grows.
:::

---

## CLT: What "Large $n$" Means in Practice

:::: {.three-col}
::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">Symmetric distributions</span>
Even $n = 10$–$15$ is often enough. The normal approximation kicks in quickly.
:::
::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">Moderately skewed</span>
$n = 30$ is a common rule of thumb. Check with a histogram.
:::
::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">Heavily skewed</span>
May need $n = 50$–$100$ or more. The more extreme the skew, the larger $n$ must be.
:::
::::

<br>

::: {.examplebox .fragment}
**Practical consequence.** For large $n$, we can use $z$-based confidence intervals and hypothesis tests for $\mu$ even when the parent distribution is unknown or skewed.
:::

---

## CLT — Simulation Lab in R

```{webr}
#| autorun: false

# CLT Simulator: change dist and n
dist <- "exponential"   # try: "uniform", "poisson", "exponential"
n    <- 30
reps <- 4000

draw_sample <- function(n) {
  switch(dist,
    uniform     = runif(n, 0, 1),
    exponential = rexp(n, rate = 1),
    poisson     = rpois(n, lambda = 3),
    rnorm(n)
  )
}

xbars <- replicate(reps, mean(draw_sample(n)))

# Theoretical parameters
mu_map    <- c(uniform=0.5, exponential=1, poisson=3, normal=0)
var_map   <- c(uniform=1/12, exponential=1, poisson=3, normal=1)
mu_t  <- mu_map[dist]; se_t <- sqrt(var_map[dist]/n)

hist(xbars, breaks=50, freq=FALSE, col="#00695c", border="white",
     main=paste("CLT:", dist, "| n =", n), xlab="Sample mean")
curve(dnorm(x, mu_t, se_t), add=TRUE, col="#F8766D", lwd=2)
```

## CLT Example: Poisson Sums {.scrollable}

::: {.taskbox}
<span class="label">Example</span>
Customers arrive at a bank at rate $\lambda = 4$ per minute. $X_i \sim \text{Pois}(4)$.

**(a)** What are $E[X_i]$ and $\text{Var}(X_i)$?

**(b)** For a sample of $n = 36$ one-minute intervals, find $P(\bar{X} \leq 4.5)$ approximately.

**(c)** Find $P(\bar{X} > 3.8)$ approximately.

**(d)** What sample size $n$ would make $P(|\bar{X} - 4| < 0.25) \geq 0.95$?
:::

---

## Poisson CLT — Check in R

```{webr}
#| autorun: false

mu <- 4; sigma2 <- 4; n <- 36
se <- sqrt(sigma2 / n)

# (b) P(X-bar <= 4.5)
pnorm(4.5, mean = mu, sd = se)

# (c) P(X-bar > 3.8)
pnorm(3.8, mean = mu, sd = se, lower.tail = FALSE)

# (d) P(|X-bar - mu| < 0.25) >= 0.95
# Need 2*pnorm(0.25/se_n)-1 >= 0.95
# 0.25/se_n >= 1.96  =>  se_n <= 0.25/1.96
# sigma/sqrt(n) <= 0.25/1.96
n_needed <- ceiling((2 * 1.96 / 0.25)^2)
cat("Minimum n:", n_needed, "\n")
```

- The population must be normal
- The sample size must equal exactly 30
- [The observations must be i.i.d. with finite mean and variance]{.correct data-explanation="The CLT requires independent observations, identical distribution, and finite variance. The population distribution does not have to be normal."}
- The population must be symmetric

## 4.4 Convergence in Probability

::: {.defbox .fragment}
**Convergence in Probability**

A sequence $X_1, X_2, \ldots$ converges in probability to constant $c$ if for every $\varepsilon > 0$:

$$\lim_{n\to\infty} P\!\left(|X_n - c| \leq \varepsilon\right) = 1$$

Written $X_n \overset{p}{\longrightarrow} c$.
:::

::: {.examplebox .fragment}
**Intuition.** As $n$ grows, the probability that $X_n$ is far from $c$ shrinks to zero. The sequence settles down near $c$.
:::

---

## Chebyshev's Inequality

::: {.defbox}
**Chebyshev's Inequality**

For any random variable $X$ with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$, and any $k > 0$:

$$P(|X - \mu| \geq k) \leq \frac{\sigma^2}{k^2}$$

Equivalently: $P(|X - \mu| < k) \geq 1 - \dfrac{\sigma^2}{k^2}$
:::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
**No distributional assumption.** Chebyshev's inequality holds for **any** distribution with finite variance. It is the key tool in proving the WLLN.
:::

---

## Chebyshev Example {.scrollable}

::: {.taskbox}
<span class="label">Example</span>
$X$ has mean $\mu = 10$ and standard deviation $\sigma = 3$.

**(a)** Use Chebyshev to bound $P(|X - 10| \geq 9)$.

**(b)** Use Chebyshev to bound $P(1 < X < 19)$ from below.

**(c)** Now suppose $X$ is actually $N(10, 9)$. Compute the exact probability $P(1 < X < 19)$ and compare with the Chebyshev bound.
:::

---

## Chebyshev — Check in R

```{webr}
#| autorun: false

mu <- 10; sigma <- 3

# (a) Chebyshev upper bound on P(|X-10| >= 9)
# k = 9
k <- 9
cheb_upper <- sigma^2 / k^2
cat("Chebyshev upper bound:", cheb_upper, "\n")

# (b) Lower bound on P(1 < X < 19) = P(|X-10| < 9)
cat("Chebyshev lower bound:", 1 - cheb_upper, "\n")

# (c) Exact (assuming X ~ N(10, 9))
exact <- pnorm(19, mean=10, sd=3) - pnorm(1, mean=10, sd=3)
cat("Exact (normal):", exact, "\n")
cat("Chebyshev is conservative — exact probability is higher.\n")
```

---

## 4.4.2 Weak Law of Large Numbers

::: {.defbox}
**Weak Law of Large Numbers (WLLN)**

Let $X_1, X_2, \ldots$ be i.i.d. with $E[X_i] = \mu$ and $\text{Var}(X_i) = \sigma^2 < \infty$. Then for any $\varepsilon > 0$:

$$P\!\left(\left|\bar{X}_n - \mu\right| \geq \varepsilon\right) \longrightarrow 0 \quad \text{as } n \to \infty$$

Written $\bar{X}_n \overset{p}{\longrightarrow} \mu$.
:::

::: {.warnbox .fragment}
This does **not** say $\bar{X}_n = \mu$ for large $n$. It says the probability of being far from $\mu$ goes to zero. Individual realisations can still deviate.
:::

---

## Proof Sketch: WLLN via Chebyshev

:::: {.two-col-lean}
::: {.col}
::: {.examplebox}
**Key steps**

1. $\text{Var}(\bar{X}_n) = \dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}$

2. Apply Chebyshev with $k = \varepsilon$:

$$P\!\left(|\bar{X}_n - \mu| \geq \varepsilon\right) \leq \frac{\sigma^2}{n\varepsilon^2}$$

3. As $n \to \infty$, right side $\to 0$.

4. Since probability $\geq 0$, conclude the limit is $0$. $\square$
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.thinkbox}
**What does the proof need?**

- Finite variance $\sigma^2$
- Independence (for $\text{Var}(\bar{X}_n) = \sigma^2/n$)
- Identical distribution (for common $\mu$ and $\sigma^2$)

The CLT is not required — Chebyshev alone is enough.
:::
:::
::::

---

## WLLN — Simulation

```{webr}
#| autorun: false

# Watch the running mean converge to the truth
set.seed(42)
n  <- 200
p  <- 0.5    # true mean of Bernoulli(0.5)

x     <- rbinom(n, 1, p)
trial <- 1:n
rmean <- cumsum(x) / trial

plot(trial, rmean, type = "l", col = "#619CFF", lwd = 1.5,
     ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = "n", ylab = "Running mean",
     main = "WLLN: Bernoulli(0.5) running mean")
abline(h = p, lty = 2, col = "black")
```

---

## WLLN — Multiple Paths

```{webr}
#| autorun: false

set.seed(258)
n  <- 200; p <- 0.5
cols <- rainbow(8)

# First path
x <- rbinom(n,1,p); trial <- 1:n
plot(trial, cumsum(x)/trial, type="l", col=cols[1],
     ylim=c(0,1), xlab="n", ylab="Running mean",
     main="WLLN: 8 independent paths")

# Remaining paths
for(i in 2:8){
  x <- rbinom(n,1,p)
  lines(trial, cumsum(x)/trial, col=cols[i])
}
abline(h=p, lty=2, lwd=2, col="black")
```

## Example: Poisson WLLN {.scrollable}

::: {.taskbox}
<span class="label">Example</span>
Let $X_i \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \text{Poisson}(\lambda = 3)$ for $i = 1, 2, \ldots$

**(a)** State $E[X_i]$ and $\text{Var}(X_i)$.

**(b)** Apply Chebyshev's inequality to bound $P(|\bar{X}_n - 3| \geq \varepsilon)$.

**(c)** Show that $\bar{X}_n \overset{p}{\longrightarrow} 3$.

**(d)** Simulate the convergence in R for $n = 500$ trials.
:::

---

## Poisson WLLN — Check in R

```{webr}
#| autorun: false

# (b)-(c): Chebyshev bound as function of n
lambda <- 3; eps <- 0.25; n_vals <- seq(10, 500, by=10)
bounds <- lambda / (n_vals * eps^2)

plot(n_vals, bounds, type="l", col="#F8766D", lwd=2,
     xlab="n", ylab="Chebyshev bound on P(|X-bar - 3| >= 0.25)",
     main="Chebyshev bound → 0 as n → ∞")
abline(h=0, lty=2)

# (d) Simulate
set.seed(1); n <- 500
x <- rpois(n, lambda)
plot(1:n, cumsum(x)/(1:n), type="l", col="#00695c", lwd=1.5,
     ylim=c(1,5), xlab="n", ylab="Running mean")
abline(h=lambda, lty=2)
```

##  {.quiz-question}

:::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## Visual Question

The graph shows the Chebyshev bound used in the standard proof of the Weak Law of Large Numbers. Which mathematical tool is being used?
::::

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8.6
#| fig-height: 2.05
#| fig-align: center
#| echo: false

n_vals_q <- seq(10, 500, by = 5)
eps_q <- 0.25
sigma2_q <- 3
bound_q <- sigma2_q / (n_vals_q * eps_q^2)

df_cheb_q <- data.frame(n = n_vals_q, bound = bound_q)

ggplot(df_cheb_q, aes(n, bound)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.15, colour = "#00695c") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#f9a825") +
  annotate("text", x = 330, y = max(bound_q) * 0.25,
           label = "Bound shrinks toward 0 as n grows",
           colour = "#004d40", fontface = "bold", size = 3.6) +
  labs(title = "WLLN proof idea",
       subtitle = "Control the probability of being far from the mean",
       x = "Sample size n", y = "Upper bound") +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))
```

- The Central Limit Theorem
- [Chebyshev's Inequality]{.correct data-explanation="Applying Chebyshev's Inequality to the sample mean gives an upper bound that shrinks to 0 as n grows. No normality assumption is needed."}
- Jensen's Inequality
- The Empirical Rule

##  {.quiz-question}

:::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## Visual Question

A fair die is rolled repeatedly. The running average settles near the dashed line. By the WLLN, what value does X̄ₙ converge to in probability?
::::

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7.2
#| fig-height: 2.9
#| fig-align: center

set.seed(258)

n_rolls <- 120
rolls <- sample(1:6, size = n_rolls, replace = TRUE)
running_avg <- cumsum(rolls) / seq_along(rolls)

df_diequiz <- data.frame(
  roll = 1:n_rolls,
  running_avg = running_avg
)

ggplot(df_diequiz, aes(x = roll, y = running_avg)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.05, colour = "#00695c") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 3.5, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#f9a825", linewidth = 1.1) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 120, by = 20)) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(1, 120), ylim = c(1, 6)) +
  labs(
    title = "Law of Large Numbers for a fair die",
    x = "Number of rolls",
    y = "Running average"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```

- 3
- 6
- 4
- [3.5]{.correct data-explanation="For a fair die, the expected value is (1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6) divided by 6, which is 3.5. The Weak Law says the running sample mean converges in probability to that value."}

## In-Class Example: Law of Large Numbers {.scrollable}

:::: {.two-col-wide}
::: {.col}
::: {.taskbox}
<span class="label">In-Class Example</span>
A fair coin is flipped many times. Let $X_i=1$ if the flip is heads and $X_i=0$ if the flip is tails.

The true population mean is:

$$\mu = P(\text{Heads}) = 0.5$$

**(a)** What does the running sample mean represent?

**(b)** Why does it jump around a lot at the start?

**(c)** What happens as the number of flips increases?

**(d)** Which result explains this behaviour?
:::
:::

::: {.col}
```{r}
#| fig-width: 5.8
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-align: center
#| echo: false

set.seed(258)

flips <- rbinom(300, size = 1, prob = 0.5)
running_mean <- cumsum(flips) / seq_along(flips)

df_coin_inclass <- data.frame(
  flip_number = seq_along(flips),
  running_mean = running_mean
)

ggplot(df_coin_inclass, aes(x = flip_number, y = running_mean)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.05, colour = "#00695c") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#f9a825", linewidth = 1.1) +
  annotate("text", x = 240, y = 0.54, label = "True mean = 0.5", colour = "#f9a825", fontface = "bold") +
  labs(x = "Number of coin flips", y = "Running proportion of heads") +
  ylim(0, 1) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```
:::
::::

## Law of Large Numbers - Check in R

```{webr}
#| autorun: false

set.seed(258)

flips <- rbinom(300, size = 1, prob = 0.5)
running_mean <- cumsum(flips) / seq_along(flips)

plot(running_mean,
     type = "l",
     lwd = 2,
     col = "#00695c",
     xlab = "Number of coin flips",

     main = "Law of Large Numbers")

tail(running_mean)
```

## Empirical Probability Connection

::: {.defbox}
**Empirical Probability from the WLLN**

Define indicator $X_i = \mathbf{1}[\text{event } A \text{ occurs on trial } i]$.

Then $E[X_i] = P(A)$, and by the WLLN:

$$\bar{X}_n = \frac{\text{number of times } A \text{ occurs}}{n} \;\overset{p}{\longrightarrow}\; P(A)$$
:::

::: {.examplebox .fragment}
**Coin flip.** Tossing a fair coin: $P(\text{heads}) = 0.5$. After many flips, the proportion of heads converges to $0.5$. This is precisely the WLLN at work.
:::

## Chapter Summary {.compact}

:::: {.three-col}
::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Key Distributions</span>
$N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ for continuous data; $\chi^2_k$ for variance; $t_\nu$ for small-sample means; $F_{\nu_1,\nu_2}$ for variance ratios.
:::
::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">CLT</span>
For i.i.d. data with finite variance, $\bar{X}_n$ is approximately $N(\mu, \sigma^2/n)$ for large $n$, regardless of the parent distribution.
:::
::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">LLN</span>
$\bar{X}_n \overset{p}{\to} \mu$. Sample averages settle near the population mean. Proof uses Chebyshev's inequality.
:::
::::

<br>

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
**One slide takeaway.** The CLT and LLN together justify why normal-based inference (confidence intervals, $t$-tests) works in practice. Learn the distributions now — everything in Chapters 5+ builds on them.
:::

## Bonus Example: Applying the CLT {.scrollable}

::: {.taskbox}
<span class="label">Bonus Example</span>
Let $X \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 1)$, so $E[X] = 0.5$ and $\text{Var}(X) = 1/12$.

**(a)** For $n = 48$ i.i.d. draws, find $P(\bar{X} \leq 0.52)$ approximately.

**(b)** Find $P(0.48 \leq \bar{X} \leq 0.52)$ approximately.

**(c)** Simulate the sampling distribution and overlay the CLT approximation. Do they agree?
:::

---

## Bonus Example — Check in R

```{webr}
#| autorun: false

n <- 48; mu <- 0.5; sigma2 <- 1/12; se <- sqrt(sigma2/n)

# (a) P(X-bar <= 0.52)
pnorm(0.52, mean=mu, sd=se)

# (b) P(0.48 <= X-bar <= 0.52)
pnorm(0.52, mu, se) - pnorm(0.48, mu, se)

# (c) Simulation
set.seed(42)
xbars <- replicate(5000, mean(runif(n)))
hist(xbars, breaks=50, freq=FALSE, col="#00695c", border="white",
     main=paste("CLT: Uniform(0,1), n=", n), xlab="Sample mean")
curve(dnorm(x, mu, se), add=TRUE, col="#F8766D", lwd=2)
```
